progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c09 (carboxyl and carboxylate groups; salts named "-oate", sodium ethanoate; a long chain lowers water solubility); chem-m7-c10 (the ester group; condensation and esterification, reversible); chem-m7-c11 (alkylammonium ions, one mention for cationic heads); chem-m7-c03 (polar and non-polar molecules; dispersion forces grow with chain length; hydrogen bonding in water, the water lattice; "like dissolves like"); Year 11 (ionic bonding; ion–dipole attraction when ionic compounds dissolve; precipitation reactions and net ionic equations; spectator ions); Module 5 solubility (chem-m5-g03b to g03d as the pack names: a precipitate forms when ions combine into an insoluble compound). Not assumed: soap, hydrophobic, hydrophilic, triglyceride, glycerol, saponification, micelle, emulsion, hard water, scum, detergent, anionic, cationic, non-ionic.
progression.startsWith: Locate the hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail. The video opens: Pour cooking oil into water, shake it hard, and within a minute the oil floats back up into its own layer. Add a few drops of soap, shake it again, and the mixture turns cloudy, and stays cloudy for much longer. The oil has spread through the water, ready to rinse away.
progression.stopsAfter: identifying the hydrophobic tail and hydrophilic head of a soap or detergent and the forces each makes; writing the saponification equation for a triglyceride with sodium hydroxide; explaining how soap removes grease (tails into grease, heads in water, droplets that repel, an emulsion, rinsing); writing the net ionic equation for scum in hard water; explaining why detergents work in hard water and describing anionic, cationic and non-ionic heads; comparing soaps and detergents. No surface tension, no CMC, no builders.
progression.nextLesson: comparing soap and detergent in soft and hard water in the lab (route chem-m7-p06, "Compare soap and detergent action").

teaching.task: Oil and water separate however hard you shake them, but with a little soap the oil spreads through the water and rinses away. How can one particle hold on to both oil and water, and why does soap make scum in hard water when a detergent mostly doesn't?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) oil and water separate after shaking, but with soap the mixture stays cloudy (1); (2) as with c03's hexane, oil is largely non-polar and can't join water's hydrogen bonds, so water squeezes the oil out (2); (3) soap is the salt of a long carboxylic acid (sodium octadecanoate); the acid barely mixes with water, but the salt has a charged end; the long non-polar tail (dispersion, hydrophobic) and the ionic carboxylate head (ion–dipole, hydrophilic) (3); (4) soap is made by hydrolysing a fat's three ester links with NaOH: glycerol and three soap molecules; NaOH is a reactant; the base takes the acid's proton, and the carboxylate can't re-form the ester, so it goes to completion (4); (5) in water, tails are squeezed out like oil: soap lines the surface and clusters into micelles, tails in, heads out (5); (6) tails dissolve into grease, heads stay in water, agitation makes soap-wrapped droplets whose negative surfaces repel, so they don't easily join and stay spread out as an emulsion that rinses away; emulsified, not dissolved in the water (6); (7) hard water's Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ join two soap anions each into an insoluble scum, using up soap (7); (8) detergents keep the tail and change the head: sulfonate and sulfate heads still attract Ca²⁺, but the calcium salts are much more soluble and stay dissolved; cationic heads are positive; non-ionic heads have no charge (8); (9) both clean the same way; soap is renewable and biodegradable but scums; detergents work in hard water, but many are petrochemical (9); memory aid (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: oil and water separate however hard you shake them, but with a little soap the oil spreads through the water and rinses away, so the video asks how one particle can hold on to both oil and water and why soap makes scum in hard water when a detergent mostly does not. Oil is mostly long hydrocarbon chains, largely non-polar, so like hexane it cannot join water's hydrogen bonds and is squeezed out. Soap is the salt of a long carboxylic acid with two very different ends: a charged carboxylate head that attracts water and a long non-polar tail that does not. It is made by saponification, heating a fat or oil (a triglyceride of glycerol joined to three acid chains) with sodium hydroxide. In water the tails are squeezed out, so soap gathers at the surface and forms micelles; with grease the tails dissolve into it by dispersion forces while the heads stay in the water, rubbing breaks the grease into droplets coated with heads, and the charged surfaces keep the droplets apart so they rinse away. Hard water's calcium and magnesium ions join two soap anions into an insoluble scum, while a detergent keeps the same plan with a sulfonate head that makes far less scum. Soap and detergent are compared feature by feature, and the memory aid is head in the water, tail in the grease. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Pour cooking oil into water, shake it hard, and within a minute the oil floats back up into its own layer. Add a few drops of soap, shake it again, and the mixture turns cloudy, and stays cloudy for much longer. The oil has spread through the water, ready to rinse away. So how can one substance hold on to oil and water at the same time?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Sodium palmitate, CH₃(CH₂)₁₄COO⁻Na⁺, is a soap. (a) Identify the hydrophobic part and the hydrophilic part of the palmitate ion. (b) Explain how this soap removes an oily stain from fabric during washing. Refer to the intermolecular forces involved." The skeletal formula is shown beside it in plain ink (no colours, no head-and-tail symbol). New soap (scenes use sodium stearate); tests the Must Do steps (both ends and their forces, insertion, droplets, repulsion, rinse). Crossed mistake: "The soap dissolves the oil in the water." (site card 3 Common Error). (A2) "The same volume of soap solution is added to a sample of rainwater and to a sample of tap water that contains dissolved calcium ions. The tap water turns cloudy, a white solid forms, and little froth appears. (a) Write a net ionic equation for the formation of the white solid. Use sodium stearate, C₁₇H₃₅COONa, as the soap. (b) Explain why a sulfonate detergent forms plenty of froth in the same tap water." New conditions (scene 7 uses a generic hard water sample; the site uses 350 mg/L Ca²⁺ in a household); tests the charge-balanced scum equation, spectator ions and the head-group reason. Crossed mistake: "C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻ + Ca²⁺ → C₁₇H₃₅COOCa" (charges not balanced; the pack's "balance scum charges" trap).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the structure and action of soaps and detergents" This video covers the structure of soaps and of anionic, cationic and non-ionic detergents, how soap is made from fats (saponification, as the source of the structure), the cleaning action (micelles and emulsification), and behaviour in hard water. The hands-on comparison is chem-m7-p06. this video starts by locating the hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail, and stops at explaining micelles and comparing soaps and detergents in hard water. It teaches: oil and water don't mix because water molecules hydrogen bond to each other and oil molecules (mostly long hydrocarbon chains, so largely non-polar) can't join in, so the water keeps its hydrogen bonds and squeezes the oil out into a layer (a short recall of c03's hexane layer); a soap is the sodium (or potassium) salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid (sodium stearate, C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻Na⁺), named "-oate" in its systematic name, sodium octadecanoate (c09); the long acid barely mixes with water, but in the salt one end is a charged ion; its long hydrocarbon tail is non-polar, attracts oil by dispersion forces and is hydrophobic (avoids water); its carboxylate head is ionic, attracts polar water molecules by ion–dipole attraction (and accepts hydrogen bonds) and is hydrophilic (water loving); soap is made by saponification: fats and oils are triglycerides, triple esters of glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) with three long carboxylic acids; heating with concentrated sodium hydroxide hydrolyses all three ester links, giving glycerol and three soap molecules; NaOH is a reactant (three per fat molecule), not a catalyst; the basic mixture takes the acid's proton, leaving a carboxylate ion, which can't re-form the ester with glycerol, so the reaction goes essentially to completion (contrast with c10's reversible esterification); in water, soap's tails are squeezed out like oil, so soap gathers at the surface with tails out of the water, and above a certain concentration it also clusters into micelles (tails inward, heads outward); cleaning: tails dissolve into the grease by dispersion forces, heads stay in the water, agitation breaks the grease into small droplets each wrapped in soap (grease in the core, heads outward), the droplets' negative surfaces repel each other, so they don't easily join back together, and they stay dispersed as an emulsion that the rinse carries away; the grease is emulsified, not dissolved in the water; hard water contains dissolved Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions (often from rocks such as limestone); two soap anions and one Ca²⁺ form insoluble calcium stearate, the scum (2C₁₇H₃₅COO⁻(aq) + Ca²⁺(aq) → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca(s)), using up soap, so there's less froth and more soap is needed; synthetic detergents keep the tail-and-head plan with different heads: anionic (sulfonate –SO₃⁻ or sulfate –OSO₃⁻; e.g. sodium dodecyl sulfate) which still attract Ca²⁺, but whose calcium and magnesium salts are much more soluble and stay dissolved, so far less scum forms; cationic (a positive nitrogen head, R–N(CH₃)₃⁺, like c11's ammonium ions; fabric softeners, some antiseptics); non-ionic (an uncharged polar chain that hydrogen bonds with water, so Ca²⁺ has no charge to bind); the comparison: both clean by micelles; soap from renewable fats and oils, readily biodegradable, forms scum in hard water; detergents work in hard and soft water, many made from petrochemicals (some from plant oils). Not here: surface tension and the pepper demonstration (site hook; author note b); the critical micelle concentration as a number (author note c); acid-catalysed ester hydrolysis (c10 recall only); why potassium soaps are softer (author note d); builders, enzymes and other laundry additives (author note e); phospholipid membranes (Biology); detailed environmental lifecycle and the history of branched detergents (author note f); calculations; the hands-on soap and detergent comparison and its risk table (chem-m7-p06).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c09, plus: oil and grease yellow; the soap tail pale blue; the soap head red with "−"; Na⁺ grey-amber; Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ teal; scum grey-white; water molecules soft blue with hydrogen bonds dotted violet; dispersion dotted pale blue; ion–dipole attractions as short dotted navy lines. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Why separate?", "Two ends", "Make it", "Clean it", "Hard water", "Detergents"); centre the structure or particle board, one model at a time; plates small or medium at the left or right only in scenes 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, 14 and 15. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous model leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 27 Oct by contact sheet): `m6-soap-bar-v1.png` (a cream soap bar; scene 3, small); `m7-soap-making-v1.png` (two cream soap bars beside a glass beaker holding a yellow oil layer over a clear aqueous layer; scene 4, medium); `m7-vegetable-oil-bottle-v1.png` (a clear bottle of yellow cooking oil, green cap; scenes 1 and 4, small). Not used: `m7-margarine-tub-v1.png` (the oil bottle already shows a fat source); `m7-hexane-water-heptane-tubes-v1.png` (two tubes of colourless layers; the oil layer here must read as yellow cooking oil, and the tubes have no stoppers for shaking); `m6-household-cleaner-bottle-v1.png` (a blue spray bottle; the detergent types are shown as structures, and a branded-looking product would add a fourth bright object). Four new plates (Assets). All plates small or medium, scaled uniformly only, never stretched. No human figures.
